title: The sounds of French
summary: Learn how French is spelled and said: silent endings, accents, letter teams and nasal sounds. You mostly listen; there is no French to use yet.
canDo: I can tell which final letters are usually silent.
I can read é, è, ê and ç and guess how they sound.
I can guess the sound of ou, oi, au, eau, ai and eu.
I can say nasal sounds without an 'n' sound, and link words with liaison.

lessons.title: Silent endings
lessons.goal: I can tell which final letters are silent and which are said.

notes.title: Most final letters are silent
notes.body: In French, the last letter of a word is usually **not** said. English does this too, in words like *talk*. In French it happens far more often, so a word like *petit* ends on a soft sound, not a *t*.

notes.title: Some final letters are said: c, r, f, l
notes.body: The final letters **c, r, f** and **l** are often said, so keep them in mind. Pronounce them as you would in English: a hard *k*, an *r* at the back of the throat, an *f* and an *l*.

words.tip: Sounds like 'puh-tee'. The final t is silent.
Sounds like 'grahn'. The final d is silent.
Sounds like 'pa-ree'. The final s is silent.
Sounds like 'ah-vek'. The final c is said like a 'k'.
Sounds like 'boh(n)-zhoor'. The j sounds like the s in 'measure', and the final r is said.
Sounds like 'nuhf'. The final f is said.
Sounds like 'eel'. The final l is said.

lessons.title: Accents
lessons.goal: I can read é, è, ê and ç and say roughly how they sound.

notes.title: é, è and ê change the vowel
notes.body: The accent on a vowel changes how it sounds. **é** is said like the *ay* in English *day*. **è** and **ê** are said like the *eh* in *bed*. Learn the accent with the letter, because it tells you how to say the word.

notes.title: Plain e and ç
notes.body: A plain **e** is a short, quiet sound, a bit like the *uh* in English *sofa*. At the end of a word it is usually silent. **ç** (c with a little tail) always sounds like *s*, never like *k*.

words.tip: Sounds like 'ka-fay'. The final é is said as 'ay'.
Sounds like 'treh'. The è is said 'eh' and the final s is silent.
Sounds like 'feht'. The ê is said 'eh' and the final e is silent.
Sounds like 'luh', short and quiet. It is shortened to l' before a vowel.
Sounds like 'gar-soh(n)'. The ç is said 's', and the on is nasal (see lesson 4).
Sounds like 'ay-lehv'. The é is 'ay', the è is 'eh', and the final e is silent.
Sounds like 'krem'. The è is said 'eh' and the final e is silent.

lessons.title: Letter teams
lessons.goal: I can guess the sound of ou, oi, au, eau, ai and eu.

notes.title: ou, oi, au and eau
notes.body: **ou** sounds like the *oo* in English *food*. **oi** sounds like *wa* in *want*. **au** and **eau** both sound like the *oh* in *go*. These letters are a team: read them together as one sound.

notes.title: ai and eu
notes.body: **ai** sounds like the *e* in English *bed*, so it is the same as è. **eu** is harder: it is a sound between *uh* and *ur*, made with your lips rounded as if to say *oo*. Do not worry about getting it perfect yet; listen and copy.

words.en: you (polite, or more than one person)
words.tip: Sounds like 'voo'. The final s is silent.
Sounds like 'mwah'. The oi is said 'wa'.
Sounds like 'oh'. The three letters make one sound.
Sounds like 'leh'. The ai is 'eh' and the final t is silent.
Sounds like 'duh', with rounded lips. The final x is silent.
Sounds like 'boh'. The eau is one sound, 'oh'.
Sounds like 'bluh', with rounded lips for the eu.

lessons.title: Nasal sounds & linking
lessons.goal: I can say nasal sounds without an 'n' sound, and link words with liaison.

notes.title: Nasal sounds: an, en, on, in, ain, un
notes.body: When **an, en, on, in, ain** or **un** is not followed by a vowel, the vowel is said through the nose and the *n* is **not** said. In the sound hints, *(n)* means "say the vowel through your nose", not an n.

notes.title: Liaison: linking to a vowel
notes.body: Usually a final consonant is silent. But when the next word starts with a vowel, the silent letter is said and joins the next word. This is called **liaison**. Only do it with common pairs like these, and it sounds natural.

words.tip: Sounds like 'ah(n)-fah(n)'. Both en and an are nasal, and the final t is silent.
Sounds like 'boh(n)'. The on is nasal: no n sound.
Sounds like 'va(n)'. The in is nasal: no n sound.
Sounds like 'pa(n)'. The ain is nasal, the same sound as in.
Sounds like 'uh(n)'. The un is nasal: no n sound.
Sounds like 'byah(n)'. The ien is nasal: no n sound.
Sounds like 'shyah(n)'. The ch is 'sh', and the ien is nasal.
